title: TA9-18496
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision in the claim of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX who claims to be a citizen of Sri Lanka, and is claiming refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant alleges the following:

That he belongs to the Sinhala majority in Sri Lanka. He joined the Sri Lanka (SLPF) police force as a XXXXXXXXXXXXX and he was also responsible for XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. His superior officer assigned him to work as a XXXX for Karuna group (KG) on XXXX, 2009. On XXXX night, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX house of a Tamil businessman. The Karukna people demanded extortion of Rs. 1 million, which was denied by the Tamil businessman. The KG people assaulted the Tamil, handcuffed and blindfolded him while the claimant stood by as a "silent witness".2 The Karuna people wanted the claimant XXXXXXXX XXXX, including the captive Tamil to XXXXXX, a far off place. After some distance the claimant realized that the Karuna people were kidnapping the Tamil and "what they were doing was extremely unlawful".3 He refused to comply and was "badly assaulted threatened with a weapon and told not to report to "any authority or any Human Rights organizations".4 He reported to his superior who told him to do nothing and save himself. He arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009 to XXXXXXXXXX competitions representing the Sri Lankan police and claimed protection on XXXXXX, 2009.
I find that the claimant is an excluded person pursuant to Article 1F (a) of the Convention.
In the alternate, I also find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
My reasons are as follows. ANALYSIS Identity

I find that the claimant is a national of Sri Lanka as is established by testimony and the supporting documentation filed.5 I also find that he is a Sinhala and was a XXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX. Exclusion 1F (a)
The Minister intervened in the hearing and presented evidence that the claimant should be excluded pursuant to s 98 of the Act and Article I F(a) of the Refugee Convention. The law:

Section 98 of the Act states that a person referred to in Article I F(a) of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention Refugee or person in need of protection. The relevant portion of Article 1F (a) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees6 states: F. The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: a. He has committed a crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crimes;

The generally accepted purpose of this provision is to exclude from the benefit of refugee protection persons whose conduct has breached international norms of acceptable behaviour either as a principal actor or as an accomplice in committing a crime against humanity.

Article 1F(a) applies to those who have directly committed a crime against humanity and also is carried to accomplices in the commission of such crimes as provided for in the London Charter of the International Tribunal, which states, in part, that: Leaders, organizers, instigators and accomplices participating in the formulation or execution of a common plan or conspiracy to commit any of the foregoing crimes are responsible for all acts performed by any persons in execution of such plans.7

In Mugesera, the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that a crime against humanity has three essential elements: 1. one of the enumerated proscribed acts is committed; 2. the act occurs as part of a widespread or systematic attack; and that 3. the attack is directed against any civilian population or any identifiable group.8 4. crimes against humanity include murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, and other inhumane acts committed against any civilian population, before or during the war, or persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds...whether or not in violation of the domestic law of the country where perpetrated.9

Accordingly, to qualify as a crime against humanity, the specific act or acts, alleged to have been committed, must be enumerated in the relevant international instruments10 and domestic law on crimes against humanity.

Article 7 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Rome Statute),11 the provisions of which are endorsed by Canada's Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act,12 states, in part, as follows:13 Crimes against humanity" is any of the following acts when committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of the attack: (emphasis added). (a) Murder; (b) Extermination; (c) Enslavement; (d) Deportation or forcible transfer of population; (e) Imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty in violation of fundamental rules of international law; (f) Torture; (g) Rape, sexual slavery, enforced prostitution, forced pregnancy, enforced sterilization, or any other form of sexual violence of comparable gravity; (h) Persecution against any identifiable group or collectively on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious, gender as defined in paragraph 3, or other grounds that are universally recognized as impermissible under international law, in connection with any act referred to in this paragraph or any crime within the jurisdiction of the Court; (i) Enforced disappearance of persons; (j) The crime of apartheid; (k) Other inhumane acts of similar character intentionally causing great suffering, or serious injury to body, to mental or physical health.

Paragraph 2(a) of Article 7 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, sets out the following: 2. For the purpose of paragraph 1: "Attack directed against any civilian population" means a course of conduct involving the multiple commission of acts referred to in paragraph 1 against any civilian population, pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organized policy to commit such attack.

Determining whether or not the claimant was complicit in the crimes committed by the SLPF and/or KG is essentially a question of fact which requires an assessment of claimant's personal situation. On this point, the Federal Court has listed six factors which must be considered to determine whether or not an individual is complicit in crimes against humanity, and these require fact-driven case-by-case analysis.14 * The Nature of the Organization * The Method of Recruitment * Position/rank within the Organization * Length of time in the Organization * The Opportunity to Leave the Organization * Knowledge of the Organization's Atrocities

The Supreme Court of Canada15 has stated that A criminal act rises to level of a crime against humanity if: Enumerated act has been committed, and the act was part of a widespread or systematic attack, and attack directed against any civilian population or any identifiable group of person and the person knew of the attack and knew or took risk his act comprised part of that attack.

The SCC provides further guidance by defining, Attack: Acts of violence, or acts that involves the imposition of a system such as apartheid; may or not be in the context of an armed conflict Widespread: Massive, frequent, large scale action, carried out collectively with considerable seriousness and directed against a multiplicity of victims Systematic: Thoroughly organized and follows a regular pattern on the basis of a common policy or plan involving substantial public or private resources
The SCC also stated that the person must have the intent to do the underlying act and have knowledge of the attack or impute knowledge of the attack. The Minister:

Thus it was vital for the Minister to make a case and provide evidence that there are serious reasons to consider that crimes against humanity have been committed either by the SLPF and or KG. Moreover, the Minister has to provide the claimant was complicit because either he had the knowledge or he had imputed knowledge of crimes to be complicit in the crimes against humanity.

The standard of proof for "Serious reasons for considering" is less than civil law standard of balance of probabilities but has to be more than suspicion or conjecture (Ramirez; Moreno; Sivakumar; FCA. The law is clear that the burden for the Minister is only to show a "serious possibility" which is lower test than likelihood.

Minister provided clear evidence that crime against humanity were commited both by the SLPF and the KG, and that the acts were part of a "widespread or systemic attack directed against civilian population." The attack need not be confined to the use of armed force but encompasses any mistreatment of the civilian population.16

Minister evidence includes claimant's statements from his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative and testimony that the Karuna Group (KG) helped Sri Lanka "eliminate the LTTE". He testified that he believes that the reason for him XXXX the Karuna group was to facilitate XXXXX XXXXXXXXX where the claimant will be recognized and XXXXXXXX. The claimant also testified and stated in his PIF that, * He stood by while the attempted extortion of the Tamil by the KG was in progress, * The claimant stood by while the Tamil was assaulted by the KG, and; * He stood by and allowed KG to force a blindfold the Tamil victim; * He stood by while the Tamil was forced XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX; * They went through at least one check point where they were not stopped; * He also testified that he knew the act by the KG was illegal and was aware that KG was involved in HR abuses.

In accordance with the criteria set out in Kvoka,17 I find that the claimant was at least a silent partner thus a participant in the joint criminal enterprise committed by KG and that he aided and abetted the commission of the crime.

The Minister has set out a well documented long history of crimes and nature of crimes committed by the Karuna Group against civilian populations in particular against Tamils. The Minister provided several volumes18 of objective evidence documenting crimes by the Karuna group against Tamil civilians and other Sri Lankans since the splintering of the group from the LTTE. The Minister's disclosures as well as the Board's documentary evidence19 also supports the evidence provided by the Minister. I also note that the LTTE itself has committed significant human rights abuses against Sri Lankan citizens and is listed as a terrorist organization by the Government of Canada.20
The Minister has also set out well documented evidence21 supporting a long history of brutality, torture and abuse committed by the Sri Lanka Police Force (SLPF) throughout the country.

Documentary evidence shows that the Karuna Group was formed in 2004 as a splinter group of the LTTE. It was a brutal organization but became more so with apparent state sanctions and support. Minister's counsel submitted (supported by documentary evidence) that, rape, abductions, extortion, and other indignities have been committed by the KG directly at the civilian population.

The claimant by his actions and or inactions helped the Karuna Group in arrest, beating kidnapping and transportation was complicit in acts against humanity. Even if he was assigned by his superior, the claimant knew that the KG committed crimes against Tamils and that the acts were illegal. Thus his participation and association with an organization, the KG, that has a limited, brutal purpose, even if for a short duration, creates a presumption of complicity, as found by the Federal Court in Hajialokhami.22
The defense of following an illegal order. The claimant testified that he was following an order from a superior officer.

Canadian courts23 have also stated that complicity for Article 1F(a) is a broad concept that is not limited to physical participation in crimes or the exercise of effective control over their commission. Moreover, Canadian jurisprudence states that it is not the fact of working for an organization that makes a person an accomplice; rather the fact of knowingly contributing to these activities in any manner whatsoever.24 (Emphasis added).
In addition to assisting the KG, his role as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX within the SLPF are critical.

The claimant was a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXX. His service in this organization, the SLPF, needs to be examined on the basis of six point analysis specific to the claimant as per Justice Hughes in Bedoya v. Canada cited above. * The Nature of the Organization: The Minister submits that the claimant was a member of the Sri Lanka Police Force (SPLF). The Minister accepts that SLPF is not an organization for a brutal and limited purpose. The SLPF performs numerous functions that are expected of a police force. However, commission of war crimes and crimes against humanity are incidental to its mandate and a regular part of its operations. Courts in Canada have considered such situation in Gutierrez25 and courts have found that among other organizations, regular police forces may be included in this category.26 Minister's objective evidence shows clearly that the SLPF routinely uses torture of civilians during its investigations of suspects.27 The claimant also testified that KG's relations with the SLPF were to "destroy LTTE" and that the two worked together. He testified that he read the news papers regularly and was up to date. I also note that the laws of the state also allow that statements given to the police under interrogation (evidence obtained under torture) are admissible in the courts, thus giving torture a tactic approval during police interrogations. * The Method of Recruitment: The claimant voluntarily joined the force as a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. * Position/rank within the Organization: the claimant provided conflicting information about his position/rank. At the first sitting, he testified that he was part of XXXXXXX with in the SLPF. He was assigned to XXXXXXXXXXX and his unit was the same as XXX (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) with in the SLPF. He also testified that he XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. Documentary evidence28 shows that he was "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXX", and in emergencies he XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX. He also represents SLPF in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX. However at the second sitting, he down played his role and testified that he was just a XXXXXXXXXX. His title shows XXXXXXXXXX. Not just a driver but a XXXXXXXXX (more on this in inclusion analysis). * Length of time in the Organization: The claimant joined and remained a member of the SLPF for more than X years and allegedly left the organization only on the day he left Sri Lanka to come to Canada to represent the SLPF in XXXXXXXXXXX. I note that there is no documentary evidence to support that he left SLPF or has been let go. * The Opportunity to Leave the Organization: The claimant testified that he could have left the SLPF at any time and had all the opportunities to leave SLPF. There were no restrictions or penalties on him for voluntary departure from SLPF. * Knowledge of the Organization's Atrocities: The claimant provided conflicting information about his knowledge of allegations of atrocities committed by SLPF. He testified that he knew of atrocities by the KG but not by police. He also testified that he was a regular reader of newspapers, etc.

Based on the forgoing, I find that the claimant was not an insignificant XXXXX for the SLPF as he testified during the second sitting. The claimant just by his presence and his functions provided support to the illegal acts by the KG and provided support to the structure which may have extended the ability and means available to KG and SLPF to abuse civilians.

Counsel is of the view that there was no "shared common purpose" on behalf of the principal claimant. I am not persuaded. The claimant belongs to the majority Sinhala group which also forms the government. He was an instrument of the state, in particular of the SLPF. a body well known to abuse systematically large segments of civilian populations29 in particular Tamil minority.

Based on the claimant's testimony, the evidence filed and submissions and observations, I find that there are serious reasons for considering that the claimant aided the KG and his 9 year service with the SLPF, was instrumental and committed crimes against humanity, and find, pursuant to section 98 of the IRPA, that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1F (a) of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, and thus excluded.
There the claimant is excluded. In the alternate, I have analyzed inclusion. Credibility
I find that some concerns about the claimant's testimony, thus his credibility.

In credibility assessment, I am guided by the Federal Court of Appeal that testimony given under oath is presumed to be true, unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.30 In addition, when assessing credibility, the panel is entitled to rely on its rationality and common sense. The assessment I must use to test the truth of a story of a witness is that it be in harmony with the preponderance of probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those conditions.31 Furthermore, I cannot be satisfied that, "the evidence is credible or trustworthy unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so."32

Canadian jurisprudence also guide me that the applicant who had been found to be not credible, he had failed to demonstrate a subjective fear and a need for personal protection, which a claimant must do in order to be recognized as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection (Gonulcan, Ali v MCI FC 2004). Moreover, it is well-established case law that a claimant's credibility can be of some use in meeting the requirements of section 97 (and its subsections) or the IRPA (Mgvdeladze, Zurab v MCI 2005 FC 1197).

In Gonulcan (2004 FC 392), the honourable judge Pinard wrote, 4. Such an applicant, rightly found to be not credible, at the very least, has not established the subjective fear and the need for personal protection required in order to be considered a Convention refugee or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 96 and 97, respectively, of the Act. In like circumstances, the IRB may find against a refugee claimant or a person in need of protection without having to consider his objective fear of persecution or the need to extend protection to individuals, other than himself, from his country of origin. If the Board does not believe the story, "it was not unreasonable for the Board to choose to give little weight to his documentary evidence" (Tola (2007 FC 669) ).

The claimant testified that he went into hiding after the alleged incident on XXXX, 2009 with the KG. However, he also testified that he continued to work as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXX for the SLPF until the day he left Sri Lanka on XXXXX, 2009. He continued to drive to the same office and continued with his regular duties. I find that the claimant was not in hiding as he alleges and find that he is not credible.

His Role: At the first sitting, the claimant testified that he belonged to XXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX and at the second sitting he downplayed his role significantly. He testified that his Unit and the CID were one and the same and his office was some 200 meters from the HQ of the CID. He XXXX by his estimate XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. Moreover, if he was just a XXXX, I would expect his ID card to show that he was just a XXXX. His ID card clearly shows that was a XXXXXXXXXX. He provided conflicting testimony. Moreover, I find it implausible that in 9 years; in contact with hundreds of police being trained by him, he would not know of atrocities done by the SLPF or the K.G.

What he knew: The claimant also testified at the first sitting that he was aware of the atrocities committed by the SLPF and downplayed these, in fact denied any knowledge of these. I am not persuaded by Counsel Submission that "this is not relevant." A letter33 from the Officer-in-Charge of the Criminal Investigation Department shows that the claimant is afraid of the Karuna Group because "he refused to participate in an unlawful arrest" and continues that the KG helped government to "eradicate" and "annihilate" the LTTE. This letter shows that the claimant was aware of the unlawful acts. Moreover, I find the choice of words "eradicate" and "annihilate" as if talking about pests rather than people.

What he knew: The claimant testified that he never knew of any atrocities against civilians and in particular against the Tamil minority by SLPF or by the KG. Yet he testified that he read the newspapers regularly and was up to date on the situation in his country and was not aware of any allegations against the police. The claimant also testified that he only found out that the KG and the SLPF worked together on XXXX, 2009. He also testified that he learnt only from newspapers that KG and SLPF worked together. I am not persuaded that someone who is so well read and XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX would not know that the KG and SLPF work together or that SLPF regularly uses torture in investigating suspects. I find that the claimant is not credible.

When he left SLPF: The claimant testified that he left the SLPF on the day he left Sri Lanka on XXXX, 2009. He also testified that when he arrived in Canada to be at the XXXXXXXXXXXX meet, he was still representing the SLPF. Moreover, he did not provide official documentary evidence that he resigned and his resignation was accepted or that he was let go. The burden is on the claimant to provide all supportive documents or provide reasonable explanation for their absence. In this case, I have none and thus I find that the claimant is not credible.

Letter from SLPF: The claimant provided a letter34 from Officer-in-Charge of "XXXX XXXXXXXXXX" which certifies that the claimant was retained by the SLPF as a "XXXXXXXX to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX" and states that "he can be transferred to serve as a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX". Based on this, the claimant downplayed his role as a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

Another letter35 from Officer-in-Charge of the Criminal Investigation Department shows that the claimant is afraid of the Karuna Group because "he refused to participate in an unlawful arrest". At the hearing the Panel expressed concern that the Head of the CID of the SLPF would write this. The claimant declined offer to send this for verification.
Based on the foregoing, I find that the claimant is not credibleand his claim is denied. In the alternate for inclusion, state protection is analyzed State Protection:

Canadian jurisprudence states: States are presumed to be capable of protecting their citizens, except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown. (Ward).36 The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available (Ward).37 The presumption of state protection applies equally to cases where the state (or an agent of state) is alleged to be a persecutor (Hinzman).38 To rebut the presumption of state protection, the burden is on the claimant to provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens, (absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national) (Ward).39 A claimant who alleges that the state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate (Flores Carrillo).40 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate. (Flores Carrillo).41 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful does not rebut the presumption of state protection. (Villafranca).42 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state. (Judge,43 Camacho).44 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection. (Rio Ramirez).45

In Zeferino v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 456, the court stated: 42. In Tejeda v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 438 (CanLII), 2008 FC 438, [2008] F.C.J. No. 552, at paragraph 6, a case involving a Mexican national, Justice Tremblay-Lamer stated that if no effort is made to seek protection it is hard to blame a decision-maker for concluding that the presumption has not been rebutted: 6. It is hard to blame a decision-maker for concluding that a refugee status claimant has not rebutted the presumption that government protection is available when he "has made no effort to seek government protection" (Skelly v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1244 (CanLII), [2004] F.C.J. No. 1503, 2004 FC 1244, at paragraph 51).

Thus the claimant can rebut presumption of protection with clear and convincing evidence that adequate protection would not reasonably be forthcoming. I find, on the evidence, that the claimant did not rebut that presumption. The claimant testified that he mentioned the matter to his immediate superior, who initially sent him to help the KG. The claimant was well respected and had access to the Officers-in-Charge of the CID and the prestigious "XXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX". He belongs to the majority Sinhala and is a XXXXXXXX. I am not persuaded that he has done all that is expected of him to seek state protection. Moreover, I have no documentary evidence that the authorities cannot adequately protect Sinhala majority, and that too, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.
I find that he is not credible and has not provided clear and convincing evidence that the state is unable or unwilling to provide him with adequate protection. Therefore his claim fails.
The claimant is excluded.

In alternate, his claim is rejected.
